fields.v: Regeneration / disposable implementations (concept: agents produce new implementations from artefacts preserved across replacements instead of modifying code); builds on Chad Fowler's 'regenerative software'. Version: N/A. Examples discussed: Timson (agent rewrite of 86 Go microservices), Bartz-Beielstein (module regenerated 3 times)

Artefacts preserved across replacements: requirements, interface contracts / public contract, tests and evaluations, architectural constraints and decisions, operational records (runbooks, production observations); in the Bartz-Beielstein example records of intent, decisions, public contract and evaluations

Not stated as a flow (regenerate from preserved artefacts -> verify against acceptance checks / obligations -> deploy; loops would need to preserve knowledge, verify independently, control deployment)
Not stated; raises who judges continuity if agents produce both implementation and tests; argues verification should be independent of the agents that produced the replacement

Not classifiable (the author does not classify regeneration; cites Böckeler's spec-first / spec-anchored / spec-as-source and her doubt that the latter two inherit MDD inflexibility). Closest: spec-as-source, as implementations are regenerated from preserved artefacts (reviewer's reading, not the author's)

Published examples show agents can replace implementations but do not establish that repeated regeneration is safe or economical (one is a one-time migration, the other one module). Open: what counts as continuity; what knowledge must persist (undocumented safeguards lost); whether maintenance effort shifts to the artefacts (precise specs 'start looking suspiciously like code'); risk of the same tests guiding and approving regeneration. Proposed evidence: case studies, agent traces, experiments varying the artefacts available during regeneration
